# CHAPTER 411

## THE HAND

East Hook smelled worse than south quay.

Achievement.

Less fish.

More rope rot.

Hot pitch.

Wet iron.

Old bilge.

Something chemical enough that Sori stopped breathing through nose.

"Charming."

Maro said, "Working harbor."

"That's excuse people use for smell."

Red recovery crane rose above roofs exactly where Masta said.

Big enough that I saw pulley block before yard.

Sign below:

**VENN MARINE RECOVE Y**

Missing R.

Masta had not exaggerated.

Dask would've enjoyed this.

Good he was elsewhere.

Yard occupied wedge between seawall and drydock cut.

Two recovery barges.

One narrow diving tender.

Stacks of chain.

Winches.

Floats.

Hooks.

Three open-sided sheds.

A fenced quarantine pen with warning boards.

And people.

A lot of people missing pieces.

Not everyone.

Not even most.

Enough that my eye stopped catching it as exception.

Man hauling line with left hand and iron work hook where right should be.

Woman on short rigid peg, thigh intact, moving crate labels with both hands.

Older diver with two natural legs but brace from hip to ankle.

Boy maybe seventeen with three fingers on one hand and no apparent concern.

Foreman on articulated below-knee limb, broad marine foot dark with wet grit.

There.

Not specialty shop because story wanted Greg to find one.

Specialty shop because harbor ate people slowly.

Sometimes quickly.

Winch cable.

Crane load.

Propeller.

Dock crush.

Gangrene after bad cuts.

Cold-water damage.

Wreck collapse.

Sea did not care whether body came home complete.

And Duskport was big enough to turn recurring disaster into industry.

Repair bodies.

Repair braces.

Repair tools.

Keep people working.

Maro followed my eyes.

"Makes sense."

"Yeah."

Sori said nothing.

Maybe because there wasn't joke.

At gate, clerk stopped us.

"Business?"

"Work. Maybe. Masta Venn sent me to ask."

"Sent or mentioned?"

Good harbor question.

"Mentioned. Specifically refused word referral."

Clerk smiled.

"That's Masta."

He shouted across yard.

"TAV! MASTA SENT A MAYBE!"

Man near recovery cradle shouted back.

"I'M BUSY!"

"HE HAS ONE LEG!"

"SO DO HALF OUR CUSTOMERS!"

Not half.

Point stood.

Clerk looked at me.

"He'll come."

"Tav?"

"Tavren Venn. Masta's brother."

There.

Name.

Tavren came three minutes later.

Mid-fifties.

Broad chest.

Dark skin like Masta.

Hair mostly gray and tied low.

Right ear missing top third.

Both hands present.

He wiped them on cloth already dirtier than hands.

Looked at me.

Crutches.

Bag.

Sori.

Maro.

Then back me.

"What'd she promise?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

"Said your condition clerk left."

His face changed.

"Married."

"Yes."

"Gullhaven."

"Also yes."

"No notice."

"Apparently."

"Bastard."

"She said similar."

"What can you do?"

There.

No résumé.

Good.

"Records. Field condition. Load systems enough to ask right specialist. Survey work. Some salvage-adjacent hardware. I don't know your yard."

"Magic?"

"Bronze. Not enough to sell you magic expertise."

One eyebrow.

"Good. Diving?"

"No."

"Swimming?"

"Yes. Not with this setup in working water."

"Good. Rigging?"

"Basic load sense. Not harbor-qualified."

"Ownership marks?"

"Can record. Don't know Duskport codes."

"Charge residue?"

"Observe with proper tools. Not universal appraiser."

"Useful answer."

Masta family trait.

Tavren pointed to fenced pen.

"Trial. Half day. Two copper if you finish records clean enough I don't have to redo them. One copper if I keep any useful portion but have to rebuild most. Nothing if you lie, touch quarantined hardware, or decide being clever is substitute for asking."

Two copper.

Not peg money.

Not nothing.

"What am I recording?"

"Today's shallow haul. Four pieces. Yard diver already cleared biological hazard. Charge status mixed. Ownership unresolved on two. You work under Nali."

"Nali?"

"Condition lead until I replace clerk."

"Then why need clerk?"

"Because Nali is also diver, rigging inspector, and only person here who can read old south-coast wreck marks without inventing letters. I prefer she does those jobs."

Reasonable.

"Two copper. Half day."

"If useful."

"Done."

Sori said, "Do you need records witness?"

Tavren looked at her.

"What are you?"

"Records/legal. Not applying."

"Then no."

Sori smiled.

"Excellent."

Maro asked, "Visitors allowed?"

"From rail. Don't cross yellow rope."

They left me to become employed or embarrassed.

Both educational.

Nali was woman I'd seen on articulated marine leg.

Forty maybe.

Short black curls.

Left BKA.

Her work limb had broad split foot, salt-dark fittings, leather socket covered in waxed canvas, side stay.

Basically Masta's expensive category in motion.

She walked on wet planks without drama.

Not natural gait.

Good gait.

Different.

She carried clipboard and pry bar.

Both hands.

Again.

I wanted one.

Badly.

Nali saw me looking at leg.

"Masta?"

"Yes."

"How much did she quote?"

"One silver eighteen."

Nali laughed.

"Cheap mood."

There.

Infrastructure.

"Duskport has enough demand?"

Nali looked around yard.

"You serious?"

"I'm new."

She leaned clipboard against rail.

"Port has three limbwright shops I trust, two I wouldn't let fit stool, one brace guild, shipyard clinic, sailors' mutual fund, dockers' injury pool, divers' burial fund, and a charity that mostly buys children braces and argues with adults about drinking."

"Three shops?"

"Hark & Venn does working limbs. South Arch does fancy articulated city legs and noble children. Brine Street does cheap pegs and repairs while-you-wait. Masta gets sailors, dockers, salvagers, mill hands, anyone who needs body to survive wet work."

"So not unusual."

"Losing limb? Still bad day. Getting fitted? Tuesday."

Good line.

She picked clipboard up.

"Harbor machines don't forgive sleeves, hands, feet, or timing. Sea adds infection. Before clinics got better, more people lost limbs from cuts that should've stayed cuts. Now fewer. Still enough."

"And sailors?"

"Rope crush. capstan. cargo. wrecks. boarding if they're idiots or unlucky. Storm damage. Frostbite north routes. Some come here already missing pieces because Duskport has specialists and work that will still hire them."

That last part mattered.

Not just harbor creating amputees.

Harbor attracting them.

Because adaptations existed.

Work hook.

Marine peg.

Modified ladders.

Harness jobs.

Dock unions that knew forms.

An ecosystem.

Nali tapped clipboard against my chest lightly.

"History lesson costs time. Trial started."

Right.

Work.

Yellow-rope pen held four recovered objects on draining racks.

All tagged temporary numbers.

A: iron cargo latch assembly, barnacle scars, twisted hinge.

B: brass-and-wood signal housing with cracked faceplate.

C: compact black ceramic cylinder wrapped in copper cage.

D: length of articulated chain with three pale glass inserts.

I looked at C longest.

Nali noticed.

"Don't."

"I wasn't touching."

"Good."

"What is it?"

"Your job says what it is physically, what marks are visible, what condition can be observed, what tests are authorized. Not what your imagination wants."

I liked Nali too.

Duskport problem.

Nali gave me forms.

Sections:

Recovery location.

Water depth.

Diver clearance.

Biological clearance.

Visible ownership marks.

Material.

Deformation.

Corrosion.

Charge-screen result.

Leak/heat/motion.

Handling class.

Disposition pending.

Lots of blank space.

"Do I fill recovery data?"

"Already entered from dive slate. Copy exact. Don't improve wording."

Good.

A came from old quay collapse at East Hook Three, six feet water.

B and C from same wreck pocket near **Merrin's Jaw**, twelve feet.

D snagged independently on harbor sweep line.

Nali demonstrated charge screen.

Portable forked brass frame placed near object without contact.

Three positions.

Green dull.

Amber pulse.

Red sustained.

"Green means safe?" I asked.

"No."

Good.

"Green means this screen did not detect threshold charge in this position."

"Better."

"Amber?"

"Some response. Stop and call me. Red?"

"Stop faster."

"Excellent."

A was easy.

Iron latch.

Ownership stamp partly visible under corrosion.

I copied characters I could see and bracketed uncertain segment.

Nali checked.

"Why not complete likely yard code?"

"Because likely isn't visible."

"Good."

B looked simple until faceplate shifted when rack vibrated from crane outside.

I stopped.

Nali looked.

"Why?"

"Movement not from me. Faceplate loose. Could expose interior if rack shifts again."

She nodded.

Moved rack wedge.

Authorized visual from side only.

Inside wood darkened with water.

Copper contact strips green-white at edges.

Charge screen green from front, green left, amber faint right.

I stopped.

Nali came.

Ran screen herself.

Amber again.

"Good. Mark localized residual response. No opening. Specialist later."

Not mystery.

Not my job to solve.

C black ceramic cylinder.

Copper cage.

No obvious corrosion except one dark seam.

Ownership marks none visible.

Charge screen from first position gave nothing.

Second nothing.

Third...

Fork hummed.

Not amber light.

Mechanical hum.

I froze.

Nali's hand came up immediately.

"Back."

I backed.

She looked at fork.

No light.

Hum stopped.

"Did screen touch?"

"No."

"Distance?"

"About two fingers from cage."

"Movement?"

"None observed."

"Heat?"

"Didn't touch. No visible vapor."

"Sound source?"

"Could be fork. Could be cylinder. I can't separate."

Nali looked at me.

"Good."

She put red isolation tag on rack.

Not because red screen.

Because unknown response.

Called **Torrin Glass**, charge specialist.

He arrived annoyed.

Older man with missing left eye.

Not limb.

Harbor still diversified injuries.

"What?"

Nali pointed.

"Screen hum position three, no lamp. Greg observed."

Torrin looked at me.

"Touch it?"

"No."

"Good."

He used different instrument.

Long insulated probe held near cage.

Waited.

Nothing.

Moved.

Tiny vibration.

Again.

"Resonance," he said. "Cage responding to screening fork frequency. Not stored charge. Could still have stored charge below probe threshold. Leave isolated until dry."

There.

Explanation partial.

Not secret treasure.

I wrote exact.

D chain was more annoying.

Three glass inserts, one cracked.

Ownership mark on every fourth link but two different stamps appeared.

I almost assumed repair splice.

Stopped.

Nali asked why.

"Two stamps. Could be repair, reused chain, or mixed assembly."

"Good. What do you write?"

"Both stamps, positions, no ownership conclusion."

"Good."

This work fit brain.

Not glamorous.

Useful.

By midday my forms were done.

Nali took them away without praise.

Excellent sign.

I ate dock bread and smoked fish in bits while waiting.

Maro had left rail at some point.

Sori remained because apparently watching employment interview counted entertainment.

She sat beside me.

"How bad?"

"I like it."

"That's bad."

"Very."

She looked toward Nali's leg.

"I get shop now."

"Yeah."

"Three trusted shops."

"Apparently."

"Harbor destroys people."

"And employs them after."

Sori chewed bread.

"That's darker."

"Also better."

"Both."

There.

Human problem without needing speech.

System hurts.

System adapts.

People keep working because rent exists.

Some because they want work.

Some because sea is only thing they know.

Some because body changed, not person.

Nali came over.

"Tavren wants you."

"Good wants or bad wants?"

"He always looks like bad wants."

Tavren was in shed office with my forms.

He had marked three spots in charcoal.

"A. You wrote ownership stamp partial. Why not infer full?"

"Couldn't see full."

"B. Amber right. Why no probable source?"

"Didn't know."

"D. Two ownership stamps. Why no likely repair note?"

"Could be repair. Could be reused links. I didn't inspect joins under authority."

He stared.

Then nodded once.

"Nali says same."

He put two copper on desk.

There.

Pay.

"Useful."

I picked up copper.

Twenty-one to twenty-three.

Equal Vale again.

"More work?"

Tavren leaned chair back.

"Maybe."

Of course.

"Tomorrow we have wreck lift outside breakwater. Old coastal courier **Merry Wake**. Sank eight years ago. Owner finally sold salvage rights after insurance fight. We recover two cargo-room safes, steering hardware, whatever loose fittings remain. Divers bring up. Yard records."

"Condition clerk work?"

"Partly. More crowded. Ownership tags matter because salvage contract excludes personal effects and temple cargo. Anything marked passenger cabin goes separate custody. Anything with temple seal stays underwater until temple observer arrives."

There.

Human conflict seed already.

"Pay?"

"Three copper full day if you're records only and useful. Four if you also do shore-side load tally and don't slow riggers. Five if Nali signs you for both plus evening custody inventory."

Better.

Not silver tomorrow.

Several days could matter.

Living costs matter too.

"How many days work?"

"Merry Wake maybe three if weather holds. Then East Hook quay collapse. Then whatever sea breaks next."

"I want several."

He looked at my crutches.

Then at me.

"For leg?"

Masta told him.

Or obvious.

"Yes."

"Masta prices mean you're short."

"Very."

"Good. Desperate workers lie. Don't."

There.

"I won't."

"Also don't work hungry to save faster. Nali will notice and send you home."

Masta family.

Annoying.

"Understood."

Tavren pushed form across desk.

Temporary yard hand.

Three-day trial.

No guaranteed hours beyond posted recovery.

Base 3c full useful records day.

Add-ons only assigned and signed.

Personal gear liability mine.

Yard covers assigned protective equipment.

No diving.

No live-load riding.

No unsupervised charge handling.

No salvage claim simply because I noticed value.

Excellent clause.

I signed.

Sori read before I did because she was Sori.

"Fine," she said.

Tavren looked at her.

"You his lawyer?"

"No."

"Good. Lawyers expensive."

"So are mistakes."

He considered.

"You want work?"

"No."

"Good."

We left yard with two new copper and tomorrow's start before first bell.

East Hook looked different now.

Still smelled terrible.

But I could see network.

Limbwright shop west.

Recovery yard east.

Dock clinic behind crane row.

A man with work hook buying noodles.

Nali crossing wet plank on marine foot while carrying clipboard and pry bar.

No one applauded.

No one stared.

Duskport had enough broken bodies that adaptation had become ordinary commerce.

Sad reason.

Useful result.

I thought about Carrow.

Could I have gotten fitted there eventually?

Probably some version.

Maybe imported.

Maybe general brace maker.

But here, harbor generated enough need for people to get very good at specific problem.

Wet grip.

Salt fittings.

Drainage.

Deck angle.

Rope work.

Ladders.

Sockets that had to survive sweat and rain and twelve-hour shifts.

Specialization followed repeated pain.

Civilization did that sometimes.

Turned injury into profession.

Not beautiful.

Still better than pretending injury was rare because it made people uncomfortable.

Sori nudged me.

"You're doing face again."

"Which?"

"Math."

I counted.

Twenty-three copper.

Travel limb one silver eighteen.

Tomorrow three to five if useful.

Bed one copper if Anchor's End still same.

Food bits mostly.

Vale twenty-three waiting back home.

No conversion.

No shortcut.

Just days.

"Three-day trial," I said.

"I heard."

"Maybe more after."

"I heard."

"Could get there."

Sori looked at me carefully.

"Eventually."

"Yes."

Not soon.

Good.

Soon would've been cheap.

We walked back toward city center.

Sea wind behind us.

Recovery crane ahead of memory.

Tomorrow wreck.

Tomorrow other people's property under eight years of water.

Tomorrow workers who knew things I didn't.

I had two copper more than morning.

And a job for three days if I stayed useful.

Peg still impossible today.

Less impossible than yesterday.

That was enough.
# CHAPTER 412

## THE TALLYMAN

Sea work started before sunrise because apparently oceans also hated reasonable hours.

I reached East Hook in dark blue light with Maro carrying breakfast and Sori carrying opinions.

Dask was asleep.

Coward.

Venn Marine Recovery already looked awake.

Lanterns along quay.

Recovery barge loaded.

Divers checking lines.

Riggers testing winch brake.

Nali stood on wet planks with one foot planted on broad split sole of her marine limb and other on crate.

Clipboard under arm.

Coffee in hand.

She looked at me.

"Early."

"You said before first bell."

"Most people hear 'before' and negotiate emotionally."

"I can complain while punctual."

"Good."

Tavren came from office.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Today you tally."

Four copper possibility.

There.

He pointed to long board hanging beside launch ramp.

Columns.

**ITEM**

**LIFT POINT**

**EST. WET WEIGHT**

**ACTUAL CRANE SCALE**

**CONDITION CLASS**

**CUSTODY**

**YARD DESTINATION**

"You keep shore-side load tally and condition intake," Tavren said. "Nali owns condition calls. Jerr owns rigging. You do not tell divers how to dive. You do not tell crane how to crane."

"Understood."

"If counts disagree, stop handoff before object leaves marked lane."

"Yes."

"If temple mark appears, nobody lifts unless observer present."

"Yes."

"Personal effects separate."

"Yes."

"If you get clever, do it quietly enough that nobody dies."

"Reasonable."

He walked away.

Nali said, "That was basically affection."

"I'm learning dialect."

Merry Wake lay outside east breakwater.

I never saw whole wreck.

Only marker buoy and recovery lines disappearing into gray water.

That was more interesting somehow.

Ship had sunk eight years ago after hull breach in winter storm.

No heroic legend.

No famous treasure.

Courier ship.

Cargo.

Mail.

People.

Insurance fight afterward lasted longer than vessel had sailed.

Now salvage rights finally sold.

Venn had contract for specified hardware and cargo-room safes.

Families still held claim windows on identified personal effects.

Temple cargo excluded pending observer.

Nothing clean.

Good.

First lift came up as steering quadrant segment.

Heavy bronze arc crusted green.

Divers had tagged **MW-SH-1**.

Jerr's crane crew landed it inside yellow intake lane.

Scale called eighty-six wet.

I wrote eighty-six.

Not eighty-five because it looked like eighty-five.

Growth.

Nali checked ownership stamp under growth.

Courier company mark.

Condition class three.

Mechanical salvage.

Yard rack B.

Simple.

Second lift was loose fittings basket.

Third was one safe.

Safe mattered.

Small iron box, maybe knee high, two lifting eyes, one bent.

Chain came tight.

Jerr swore.

"Hold."

Crane stopped.

Diver signal line twitched twice.

Runner shouted from rail.

"Bottom snag."

Jerr adjusted angle.

I watched.

Not my craft.

After three minutes safe rose another foot.

Then something came with it.

Canvas.

Dark bundle snagged around lower corner.

Nali saw before me.

"Stop."

Crane stopped.

Bundle broke surface.

Cloth wrapped around long narrow shape.

Not cargo packing.

Too careful.

Jerr said, "Personal?"

Nali did not answer.

"Lane C," she said. "No unwrap."

Safe and bundle landed together.

Ownership problem immediately.

Safe belonged salvage contract if cargo-room manifest matched.

Bundle might not.

I wrote both as one lift but two intake objects.

Nali glanced.

"Good."

Little things.

Paid little things.

A yard clerk named **Hessa Brin** came over from custody table.

Not my Hessa.

Probably.

Did not ask.

She wore blue cord around sleeve meaning family-claim custody.

"Bundle goes sealed rack."

Nali nodded.

A man outside yellow rope shouted.

"That's mine."

There.

Human problem arrived before breakfast finished.

Man maybe forty.

Weathered coat.

Red eyes.

Not drunk.

Or not only drunk.

He pushed to rope.

Worker blocked him.

"Back."

"That is my brother's."

Nali looked at him.

"Name?"

"Toren Vale."

Of course Vale.

Sori, farther back, physically turned away.

I almost laughed.

Wrong moment.

Toren pointed at bundle.

"That wrap. My mother stitched those blue corners. Eren carried charts in it."

Hessa Brin said, "Claim registry?"

"Filed six years ago."

"Number?"

"I don't carry dead brother's paperwork in pocket."

"Then we verify before release."

"You have it right there."

"And if you're wrong?"

He slapped chest.

"I'm not."

Could be true.

Could be grief making certainty.

Could be both.

Nali said, "Nothing leaves wet intake until cataloged."

Toren looked at her.

"I've waited eight years."

There it was.

Procedure versus somebody's life again.

Different shape.

Not emergency.

Still sharp.

"I know," Nali said.

"No, you don't."

Her face did not change.

"No. I know policy."

That answer was honest.

Also bad.

Toren's eyes went to bundle.

"You tear that open and dump his things on table, I swear to every god in this harbor..."

Hessa Brin stiffened.

"Nobody said dump."

"That's what yards do. Inventory. Photograph. Assign lot."

"Family effects don't become auction lot."

"Unless you decide it isn't his."

There.

He wanted one thing badly.

Not value.

Not money.

He wanted brother's bag back intact.

Custody process wanted identity established before release.

Both reasonable.

Nali looked at me.

Not because I was authority.

Because I was holding tally.

"Record dispute. Do not move bundle until custody review."

I wrote exactly that.

Toren saw.

"You're writing?"

"Yes."

"Write it's his."

"I can't."

"Of course."

Tessa echo.

Everybody knows how to explain why they can't help.

I hated that line now.

Useful line.

Hated it.

I looked at bundle.

Blue corners visible.

Canvas water-dark.

One brass strap buckle under growth.

Maybe ownership mark without opening.

"Can we examine exterior only?" I asked Hessa.

She looked at Nali.

Nali looked at custody line.

"No opening," Hessa said. "No cutting. No contents exposure. Exterior handling permitted with witness if crane lane clears."

Better question.

Not solution.

We moved bundle separately onto slatted table.

Toren stayed behind rope.

Hessa present.

Nali present.

I did not touch until told.

Exterior had blue cross-stitch corners.

Four.

One mostly rotted.

Buckle greened over.

Leather strap stamped faintly.

I wet cloth and cleaned only stamp face.

Letters:

**E. VA...**

Could be Vale.

Could be Varn.

Could be half a dozen names.

Toren saw from rope.

"Eren Vale."

Hessa said, "Maybe."

He flinched like she'd hit him.

I understood why.

Maybe was accurate.

Still cruel word after eight years.

I looked at stitch pattern.

"Claim file might include description?"

Hessa nodded slowly.

"If family filed identifying details."

"Can runner pull file while object stays sealed?"

"Yes."

"Do that."

Toren snapped, "I told you."

"I know."

"Then why file?"

"Because if it matches your claim, nobody has to open it to prove enough."

He stopped.

There.

Not perfect.

Possible.

Hessa sent runner.

We resumed recovery.

Work did not pause for grief.

That felt wrong.

Also necessary.

Second safe came up clean.

Then steering linkage.

Then two sealed brass cylinders from cargo locker.

Portable charge screen showed no active response.

Temple observer had not arrived yet.

No temple seal.

Standard cargo.

Condition three.

Rack C.

My board filled.

Wet weight.

Dry estimate blank until later.

Custody marks.

Dispositions.

Then diver bell rang hard.

Three fast.

Every worker changed.

No shouting first.

Just movement.

Jerr locked crane.

Tender crew hauled signal.

Nali was already toward ladder.

I did not know code.

Maro did not either.

Sori went still.

A diver surfaced wrong.

Too fast.

One arm over line.

Helmet half flooded.

Tender grabbed harness.

Second diver came up behind helping.

They got first onto platform.

Worker yelled, "Leg cut!"

Blood in water.

Not much visible.

Enough.

Tavren appeared from nowhere.

"Clinic. Now."

No Greg.

No hero.

Qualified people moved.

I backed lane clear.

That was useful.

Then I saw problem on my board.

Current lift line still attached below.

Crane load status uncertain.

If emergency crew forgot, somebody might move equipment with live line.

I wrote **HOLD - DIVER INCIDENT / LINE STATUS UNKNOWN** in giant letters and clipped red tag to crane tally hook.

Jerr saw.

Nodded.

"Good."

Tiny.

Useful.

Diver's name was **Pella Ro**.

Cut from torn hull edge through suit at calf.

Not amputation.

Not yet anything dramatic.

Clinic cart took her.

Nali returned five minutes later with wet hands.

"Stable enough. Deep cut. They think tendon spared."

She flexed her own left knee absent-mindedly.

Not symbolism.

Worker knowledge.

"Recovery pauses until line inspected," she said.

Jerr agreed.

Tavren looked at sky.

Money disappearing by minute.

Nobody argued.

Procedure clean because danger clear.

Human cost still there.

Pella would lose work days at minimum.

Maybe more.

Dock injury pool covered some.

Nali said it without speech.

Another reason limbwrights existed.

Another reason funds existed.

Not because harbor romantic.

Because harbor hurt people often enough to build institutions around damage.

Toren Vale was still waiting.

Runner returned during pause with claim file.

Hessa read.

"Blue cross-stitch corners, four. Brass buckle stamped E. VALE. One leather chart wrap, narrow. Mother listed as Sela Vale."

Toren stopped breathing.

Hessa looked at bundle.

Then at file.

"Exterior match sufficient for provisional family identity."

"Provisional?"

"We still need signature and release witness."

"But no opening?"

"No opening required for identification if you accept sealed contents as-is."

He nodded too fast.

"Yes."

Hessa said, "If later there's someone else's property inside, you inherit reporting obligation."

"Yes."

"If there is hazardous material, you report."

"Yes."

"If seal breaks before release stamp..."

"I won't touch it."

His voice cracked.

There.

He did not thank us.

Good.

He shouldn't have to.

He had waited eight years for people doing their jobs.

Hessa moved bundle to family rack under seal.

Toren walked beside rope like it might disappear again.

I watched too long.

Nali tapped board.

"Tallyman."

"Right."

Work resumed after line inspection.

No hidden monster.

No ancient curse.

Just ship broken under water and humans trying to extract pieces without adding bodies.

By midday I understood why recovery paid better than simple records.

Every object crossed three systems at once.

Weight.

Condition.

Ownership.

Sometimes hazard.

Sometimes memory.

Sometimes all of them.

A corroded hinge was hinge until stamp made it evidence.

A sealed bag was canvas until man behind rope recognized mother's stitching.

A bronze cylinder was scrap until temple seal said absolutely not.

That one arrived after lunch.

Temple observer still twenty minutes away.

Diver sent up slate first:

**MARK FOUND / LOWER LOCKER / TEMPLE SUN-THREE**

Tavren immediately canceled lift.

Client representative objected.

First time I met him.

**Sel Marr**, salvage-rights broker.

Clean boots.

Bad sign in recovery yard.

"Contract says cargo-room recovery."

Tavren said, "Temple exclusion says mark stays submerged pending observer."

"It's already rigged."

"Then it can stay rigged."

"We're paying diver time."

"Yes."

"Every minute costs."

"Yes."

"You could bring it to surface and leave sealed."

"No."

Sel looked at Nali.

"Your view?"

"No."

Then at me.

Why me?

Because new face sometimes looked flexible.

"You did records on this contract?"

"Today."

"Does bringing sealed cargo up alter custody?"

I knew enough now.

Not enough to answer broad.

"Contract says stays underwater until observer. Surface violates literal condition."

"Literal."

There was disdain in word.

"Yes."

"Do you think it matters?"

Human question disguised as technical.

"I don't know why temple required it."

"Exactly."

He smiled like I'd helped.

"So maybe it doesn't matter."

"Or maybe that's why it does."

Smile gone.

Good.

Sel said, "You people love uncertainty when somebody else pays for it."

Toren echo in different clothes.

Everybody had line.

Tavren said, "Observer is twelve minutes out now."

"Twenty became twelve."

"Time works."

Sel swore and walked away.

No grand conflict.

Just money versus custody rule whose reason wasn't visible.

Correct procedure won this one.

Maybe rightly.

Still cost somebody.

Observer arrived eleven minutes later.

Temple woman named **Iri San**.

She checked mark underwater through diver slate and surface lens.

Then authorized lift into separate blue-rope lane.

Reason for underwater rule turned out boring and sensible.

Certain old temple shipping seals used water-pressure fracture paint. If broken cargo was lifted dry before observer saw pattern wet, evidence could vanish.

There.

Unknown reason had actual reason.

Sel looked annoyed.

Not embarrassed.

People rarely rewarded universe for proving them wrong.

Object came up.

Ceramic chest with sun-three seal, one corner cracked.

Fracture paint feathered around crack underwater-blue.

Iri photographed/sketched before drying.

Then custody transfer.

I wrote what I was told.

Not story of gods.

Condition.

Custody.

Weight.

By late afternoon my right hand cramped from writing.

Shoulder held.

Crutches were annoying on wet planks because every tally move meant board, pencil, crutch, body.

More hands.

Again.

Nali moved through same yard with clipboard in one hand and pry bar in other.

Her marine limb clicked softly on wet boards.

Not magic.

Not effortless.

Twice she stopped to retighten socket strap.

Once she sat and rubbed stump through canvas because day was long.

Still had two hands.

I wanted one more than morning.

Badly.

Tavren reviewed tally at sunset.

He checked weights against crane sheet.

One mismatch.

Mine said forty-two.

Crane sheet forty-seven.

I traced item.

Loose fitting basket had drained before my second notation.

Wet scale initial forty-seven.

I had copied later rack weight forty-two into wrong column.

Mistake.

There.

Not hypercompetent perfection.

I corrected with strike-through, initial, note.

Tavren watched.

"Why?"

"Wrong column. Rack weight after drain."

"Could've made crane sheet wrong."

"Could have. It wasn't."

He nodded.

Next.

No shame ceremony.

Good workplace.

Nali checked condition entries.

"Useful."

Tavren checked red hold tag after diver incident.

"Who put that?"

"Me."

"Good."

Then family-dispute note.

"You solved?"

"No. Claim file matched exterior enough for custody to release sealed later."

"Better answer."

He counted coins.

Four copper.

Assigned load tally and useful records.

No evening inventory.

Exactly contract.

Twenty-three to twenty-seven.

There.

Four copper closer to silver I could not yet count toward because conversion remained unstated.

Still closer.

Maybe.

Definitely more money.

Tavren said, "Tomorrow same wreck. Weather good. Pella out. Crew short. You do same unless Nali changes."

"Okay."

"Third day maybe quay collapse if divers finish."

"Okay."

He looked at my crutches.

"Masta fitting you?"

"Not yet."

"Saving?"

"Trying."

"Don't rush deposit."

Family trait.

"She said same."

"She usually right when expensive."

"Good to know."

He left.

Nali sat on crate loosening side stay on her limb.

"First full day?"

"Yes."

"Feet hurt?"

"One foot. Hands more."

She laughed.

"Work leg won't fix work."

"I've been lied to."

"Masta definitely didn't lie."

"No."

She rubbed scar line through socket edge.

"You still want one?"

I looked at board.

Wet yard.

Two crutches leaning against crate.

My hands sore from moving everything around them all day.

"More."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Means you saw bad parts too."

There.

That mattered.

She strapped limb back.

Stood.

"Tomorrow bring gloves. Yard issue pair sucks."

"I don't own recovery gloves."

"Then use yard pair and complain. Harbor tradition."

I could do that.

At Anchor's End that night, Dask had three mirror pamphlets and no new mirror.

Sori looked at four copper.

"Twenty-seven."

"Yes."

"Still not enough."

"Yes."

"You look happy."

"Annoying, isn't it?"

Maro asked, "Good day?"

I thought about Pella bleeding into sea.

Toren waiting beside rope.

Temple chest staying underwater while money burned.

One wrong number on my tally.

Four copper.

Nali rubbing stump at end of shift.

"Useful day," I said.

That was more accurate.

Tomorrow before first bell again.

Merry Wake still under water.

My leg still missing.

Money still not enough.

Fine.

All three were things I could work with.
# CHAPTER 413

## THE DRINKER

Duskport was famous for beer.

Apparently.

Nobody had mentioned this until I was already drinking it.

That felt dishonest.

"Why does it taste like rope?"

Sori lowered her cup.

"Rope tastes better."

Maro swallowed with face of man accepting medical procedure.

"Smoke."

"There's smoke," I agreed.

"And salt."

"Beer should not have salt."

Dask sniffed his.

"I think that's mineral."

"You think everything is mineral when you don't know."

"That's not true."

"Name three things."

He looked at beer.

"This may be mineral."

Good.

We had been told to come here by six different people.

Not one recommendation.

Six.

Pell Varo at Anchor's End.

Nali.

A fish seller.

A porter who had never spoken to us before.

Dask's mirror-guild woman.

And an old sailor who overheard Sori ask where people went after work and shouted, "Black Keel!" from across street like city had appointed him.

The Black Keel sat three streets inland from East Hook.

Low ceiling.

Black beams.

Long tables scarred by knives, mugs, hooks, and one circular burn mark large enough to have story.

A ship's bell hung over bar.

Every wall carried brewery plaques.

**DUSKPORT BLACK**

**OLD BREAKWATER STOUT**

**SALT HOUSE NINE**

**THREE ANCHORS STRONG**

**GULL'S REGRET**

That last one should have warned me.

Bartender asked if first time.

Sori said yes.

He smiled.

Not kind smile.

Then brought four squat mugs of **Old Breakwater Strong**.

"Local," he said.

"Good?" I asked.

"Local."

Second warning.

I drank anyway.

Now here we were.

"Why is Duskport famous for this?" I asked.

Woman beside us turned around.

"Because it survives ships."

She had one eye, both arms, and enough shoulders for three people.

"What does that mean?"

"Strong. Keeps. Doesn't turn on long runs. Water goes bad, weak beer goes sad, Breakwater stays angry."

"It tastes angry."

"That's how you know it's working."

She raised mug.

I looked at mine.

"How strong?"

Bartender, somehow listening from fifteen feet away, called:

"Strong enough."

Everyone nearby laughed.

Fucking city.

This was after second Merry Wake day.

Which had started before sunrise with rain.

Not storm.

Harbor rain.

Cold enough to make wood slick and everyone mean.

Pella was out.

Jerr had one fewer diver than planned.

Tavren looked at sea, looked at crew, and cut target list in half.

Good employer.

Annoying for money.

I reported with right hand still stiff from yesterday's writing.

Nali handed me waxed slate instead of paper.

"Rain."

"I noticed."

"You'd be surprised."

She had different foot on today.

Same socket and side stay.

Narrower sole with deeper cross-grooves.

I noticed.

She noticed me noticing.

"Wet deck foot."

"You change feet?"

"Sometimes."

"How long?"

"Two minutes if clean. Ten if sand gets in lock. Forty if angry."

"The foot?"

"Me."

Good.

Then work.

Merry Wake gave us steering housing first.

Then a copper-bound locker with no personal mark.

Then half a deck winch that weighed enough to make crane complain.

Greg did not become exciting.

I tallied.

Nali conditioned.

Jerr swore at rain.

Tavren swore at insurance paperwork.

Sori had come to watch first lift and somehow ended up helping Hessa Brin copy custody numbers because Duskport apparently converted visitors into labor if they stood still too long.

Maro left after breakfast to see coastal herb market.

Dask returned from mirror guild with a pamphlet nobody asked for.

Normal.

Then near third bell, diver slate came up with:

**LOWER CABIN / BRASS CASE / BLUE MARK / FIXED UNDER BENCH / OWNER UNKNOWN**

Tavren read it.

"Blue mark shape?"

Runner shrugged.

"Slate says blue."

"Useful."

Second slate ten minutes later.

**OVAL BLUE / THREE WHITE CUTS / CASE BOLTED / CAN REMOVE BENCH OR CASE**

Nali stopped.

"Three cuts?"

Hessa looked up from custody table.

"Courier medical."

Tavren said, "Maybe."

Hessa nodded.

"Maybe."

There.

People learning.

Old courier emergency medical cases used blue oval with three white slash marks in some routes.

Not all.

Merry Wake had carried passengers and dispatch cargo.

Eight years underwater.

Case could contain nothing.

Could contain spoiled supplies.

Could contain charged medical hardware.

Could belong to ship.

Could have been personal physician kit.

Salvage contract did not specifically list medical equipment.

Sel Marr appeared within twelve minutes because money sensed hesitation.

"If it's bolted to ship, fixture."

Hessa said, "Not necessarily."

"Bolted."

"So are private lockboxes."

"Under bench."

"People bolt things under benches."

Sel looked at Tavren.

"Lift it. Determine after."

Tavren looked at Hessa.

Hessa looked at contract.

Then me.

Why me?

I was tally.

"Any old manifest category?" I asked.

She flipped pages.

"Merry Wake manifest lists one ship medical cabinet under operating equipment. No serial. One passenger physician, Dr. Alen Marr, declared professional kit at embarkation. No description."

Sel's face changed.

Small.

Marr.

There.

"Relation?" Sori asked from custody table.

Sel looked at her.

"Grandfather."

Oh.

Good.

Human problem had arrived for work.

"He died on Wake?" I asked.

"Yes."

Sel folded arms.

"And before anyone gets sentimental, salvage company bought rights. My family claim lapsed decades ago."

"Eight years," Hessa said.

"Feels decades."

"Claim window closed six years ago."

"Exactly."

Sori watched him.

"You don't want it?"

Sel's jaw moved.

"I want contract executed."

Not answer.

Nobody pushed.

Tavren asked, "Can divers identify mount without disturbing case?"

Jerr said yes.

Next slate:

**CASE HAS OWN BASE PLATE. BASE PLATE BOLTED TO BENCH. QUICK RELEASE CORRODED CLOSED.**

That changed things.

Ship fixture could be base plate.

Case could be removable equipment.

Or ship equipment designed removable.

Still not answer.

Sel said, "Cut release. Lift case."

Hessa said, "Custody class first."

"How? Underwater?"

"We can hold."

"Holding costs me."

There.

Again.

Tavren looked at rain.

Divers had limited bottom time.

Weather window narrowing.

If we spent twenty minutes debating one case, second planned winch lift might die for day.

That cost yard.

Cost Sel.

Cost crew opportunity.

If we lifted uncertain case into wrong custody lane, could compromise claim.

Correct procedure did not hand us clean answer.

Sori asked, "Is there a neutral action?"

Hessa said, "Photographic slate if diver has plate."

Jerr shook head.

"Plate topside."

"Send down?"

"Ten minutes rig, maybe."

Sel laughed once.

No humor.

"Ten minutes for picture of box."

I looked at him.

"You care."

He looked at me.

"Don't."

"Okay."

I stopped.

Not my story to pry open because surname appeared.

Tavren made call.

"Send plate. We lose second winch if we lose it."

Sel said, "That's my salvage day."

"Yes."

"I'm paying for it."

"Yes."

"And you're choosing picture over recoverable hardware."

"Yes."

Tavren did not explain himself into innocence.

That mattered.

Plate went down.

We waited.

Rain tapped crane hood.

Nali adjusted left socket once.

I held slate under coat.

Picture plate returned with case image.

Blue oval.

Three white cuts.

And along lower corner, almost gone:

**A. MARR / PHYS.**

Sel stared.

Nobody spoke.

Hessa said, "Personal professional property. Family claim expired. Under salvage contract, unclaimed personal effects transfer to insurer estate, not salvage buyer."

Sel closed eyes.

"Of course they do."

Sori said softly, "You can file descendant petition."

"I know."

"Different from salvage claim."

"I know."

There was anger in second one.

Not at her.

Maybe everyone.

Tavren said, "Lift?"

Hessa considered.

"Authorized to family-custody rack under insurer estate. Sealed. No opening."

Sel laughed again.

"So my company pays divers to recover my grandfather's case so insurer can hold it while I petition them to give it to me."

Nobody had useful response.

Because yes.

That was exactly what happened.

"Fuck me," he said.

Nali said, "Probably separate form."

He looked at her.

Then laughed for real.

Small.

Needed.

Case came up.

I recorded wet weight.

Ownership mark.

Custody destination.

No condition opening.

Sel stood six feet away and did not touch it.

When Hessa sealed family rack, he said:

"My mother said he carried silver instruments."

Not to anyone.

Then walked off.

We lost second winch.

Tavren paid crew anyway.

Not full extra work because not performed.

Fair.

Late afternoon we did custody inventory because rain shut further lift.

Nali assigned me.

There.

Potential fifth copper.

Inventory was less exciting than wreck.

Which meant dangerous.

Excitement kept brain awake.

Inventory made numbers become furniture.

I checked tags.

Rack positions.

Seal counts.

Weight sheet references.

One mismatch.

Not dramatic.

Temple chest listed blue lane rack 4 on intake sheet, physically rack 5 because rack 4 had drainage leak.

Move had been authorized.

Record not updated.

I found move chit clipped under Hessa's board.

Corrected cross-reference.

Second mismatch was mine.

Yesterday's loose fitting basket had two sub-bags, not one.

I had recorded combined disposition without sub-bag count.

Nali made me fix it.

Good.

Third was not mismatch.

I thought it was.

Safe A seal number looked 7716.

Custody sheet 771G.

I stared too long.

Hessa said, "Old stamp. G has flat tail."

"That's terrible."

"Yes."

"Why use it?"

"Because city bought nine thousand seals before anyone complained."

Economy.

Beautiful enemy.

At end, Nali signed both day records and custody inventory.

Tavren counted five copper into hand.

"Useful."

Twenty-seven to thirty-two.

There.

Five copper.

Largest single day's ordinary earned pay in current life, I thought.

Maybe.

Would need records.

Did not claim.

Thirty-two copper.

Still not enough.

Much closer to eighty-four.

Still silver problem beyond that.

Good.

Then Nali said, "Beer."

"What?"

"You worked two days at East Hook. Duskport requires beer."

"Law?"

"Worse. Culture."

Tavren, passing behind her, said, "Black Keel."

"Why?"

"Beer."

"Good?"

He kept walking.

"Strong."

Third warning.

At Anchor's End, Pell Varo asked how yard went.

"Useful."

"Then Black Keel."

"Why does everyone say that?"

"Beer."

"Good?"

"Duskport."

Fourth warning.

Maro returned smelling like herbs.

Dask returned carrying pamphlet titled **REFLECTIVE FABRICATION STANDARDS OF LOWER COASTAL GUILDS, ABRIDGED**.

Sori had ink on fingers from custody forms.

I said, "Apparently we have to drink beer."

Maro said, "Good."

Dask said, "Duskport beer is famous."

"How do you know?"

"Mirror guild told me."

Of course.

Sori said, "One."

"One what?"

"Beer. I am not carrying any of you up twelve stairs."

"I can climb."

"Sober."

"Also drunk."

"Not experiment."

So Black Keel.

Old Breakwater Strong.

Rope beer.

The one-eyed woman introduced herself as **Hena Quill**, deck boss from north-coast grain ship.

She explained Duskport beer while insulting us for not knowing.

Port had been brewing strong dark beer for generations because grain came downriver, salt ships needed something that kept, and harbor water historically tasted like metal in summer.

Brewers roasted grain hard because damp storage spoiled lighter malt more easily.

Then sailors developed taste for it.

Or claimed they did.

Then breweries competed over strength.

Then Duskport started exporting barrels.

Then reputation became fact because enough people repeated it.

"So it's famous because it doesn't spoil?" Sori asked.

Hena shrugged.

"Started there. Now famous because Duskport says so louder than everyone else."

That I believed.

"And people like taste?"

Hena took long drink.

"Some."

"Do you?"

"No."

I stared.

She grinned.

"But I'm from Duskport."

There.

City explained.

First mug tasted terrible.

Halfway through, tasted terrible warmer.

This was not improvement.

It was strong though.

Very.

I felt it behind eyes before mug empty.

Current body had different tolerance than first life.

Important data.

Sori's cheeks went red.

Maro became more talkative.

Not loud.

Just sentences longer than normal.

Dask became exactly same except faster.

Terrifying.

"The bitterness isn't actually primary problem," he said. "It's finish. There is a mineral persistence after swallow which interacts with smoke character and perhaps salt air perception. If consumed inland it might be different. We would need comparison."

Sori pointed at him.

"No experiments."

"That's not experiment. That's tasting."

"You are not taking beer inland."

"I didn't say I was."

"You just proposed inland comparison."

I laughed.

Too much.

Beer.

Hena slapped table.

"Second round."

Sori said, "No."

Bartender already pouring.

"No," Sori repeated.

Hena said, "Visitors get two."

"Why?"

"First teaches. Second forgives."

"Does it taste better?"

"No."

Honest city.

Second mugs arrived.

I should not.

Work before first bell tomorrow.

Current body.

Crutches.

Stairs.

Money target.

Responsible.

I took sip.

Still fucking horrible.

"This is worse," I said.

Maro said, "You know what's coming now."

"That's worse."

Sori drank hers and shuddered.

"I hate Duskport."

"You bought second."

"I did not buy this."

Hena raised hand.

"I bought."

Sori pointed at her.

"I hate you."

"Good. Drink."

People around us sang eventually.

Not coordinated.

Several songs at once.

One table sang ship-launch song.

Another answered with rude version.

Someone rang bell.

Bartender yelled because bell apparently had rules.

Nobody listened.

Maro told story about being twelve and falling through greenhouse roof because he tried to retrieve kite for girl who did not like him.

That was new.

"Did she like you after?" I asked.

"No."

"Did kite survive?"

"Also no."

"Successful operation."

"I broke two ribs."

Sori laughed hard enough beer came out nose.

Worth Duskport.

Dask admitted he once spent three days proving his uncle's kitchen table was tilted.

"Was it?" I asked.

"Yes."

"How much?"

"Three millimeters over length."

Sori put head on table.

"Why three days?"

"He kept moving it."

"Because you were measuring his table."

"That affected method."

I loved him a little.

Dangerous beer.

Then Sori looked at me.

"Your turn."

"No."

"Story."

"I have no stories."

Three people stared.

"Fine."

I considered first life.

Too many.

Some not funny anymore.

Some never were.

I chose one where I tried to impress a mercenary captain by jumping from stable roof at twenty-three and landed in manure because I misjudged darkness.

I left out S-class.

Did not matter.

Maro laughed before ending because he knew where story went.

Sori asked, "Did captain hire you?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Said anyone willing to commit that hard to bad idea could be pointed at enemy."

Dask nodded seriously.

"Reasonable."

"No," Sori said.

"Historically successful."

"Still no."

Second mug became half.

Then less.

I stopped there.

Not discipline exactly.

Stomach had vote.

Beer sat like smoked brick.

Strong beer plus horrible taste had natural braking system.

Maybe design.

Hena approved.

"You'll live."

"Was that uncertain?"

"First-timers sometimes try third because pride."

"No."

"Smart."

"I've been called that."

"By who?"

"Me mostly."

She laughed.

At some point work left shoulders.

That was point.

Not beer.

Not Duskport reputation.

We had been moving for days.

Survey.

Road.

White Span.

Bellweather.

Sable Quay.

Packet.

People wanting things.

Duskport.

Job.

Peg.

Money.

Wreck.

For one evening, none needed solving.

Sori stopped tracking purse.

Maro stopped watching room exits.

Dask stopped taking notes.

Actually.

He put pamphlet away.

I stopped calculating silver I did not have.

Thirty-two copper stayed thirty-two whether I stared at it or not.

We were merry.

There.

Stupid word.

Accurate.

When we finally left, Duskport air felt excellent because it did not taste like beer.

Sori walked straight.

Mostly.

Maro sang one line of launch song and forgot next.

Dask explained that forgetting lyric did not mean song lacked lyric.

I used crutches carefully.

Very carefully.

Wet cobble plus alcohol plus one leg was not place for pride.

I was not drunk enough to be stupid.

I was drunk enough to know I could become stupid.

Useful boundary.

At Anchor's End, twelve stairs waited.

Sori pointed.

"Fuck."

"Correct."

Pell Varo looked up from desk.

"Black Keel?"

"Yes."

"Breakwater?"

"Yes."

"Good?"

Four of us said, "No."

He smiled.

"Duskport."

I climbed stairs one at time.

Crutch.

Right foot.

Lift.

Crutch.

Right foot.

Lift.

Slow.

Not elegant.

Safe.

Halfway, I thought about work leg.

Then told brain to shut up.

Tomorrow.

Tonight I had earned five copper, lost argument with beer, learned Maro had once fallen through greenhouse for girl, and discovered Dask could make drunkenness sound peer reviewed.

Useful day.

Maybe good one too.

Beer remained unforgivable.
# CHAPTER 414

## THE RETAINER

Duskport beer did not improve with sleep.

That was first finding.

Second finding: head mostly fine.

Stomach annoyed.

Mouth tasted like burned rope had filed complaint overnight.

Useful.

I drank water.

A lot.

Sori was already downstairs at Anchor's End with tea and face of person who had won by suffering less.

"Morning."

"No."

"You look fine."

"I am fine. Beer is not."

Maro sat across from her eating eggs.

"I slept well."

"Traitor."

Dask arrived last carrying mirror pamphlet and looking exactly normal.

"I think bitterness may be preservative-adjacent rather than flavor-forward."

Sori pointed spoon at him.

"You are banned from describing breakfast."

Good.

I ate bread.

Kept it.

Then East Hook.

Final trial day.

That mattered more than beer.

Weather had changed.

Rain gone.

Wind up.

Not dangerous yet.

Enough to wrinkle harbor water and slap loose canvas against frames.

Tavren stood at yard gate with slate.

"Merry Wake delayed."

Nali looked past him toward sea.

"Outside chop too ugly?"

"Divers can work. Crane barge can't hold clean enough for safe heavy lift until turn."

He looked at me.

"Quay collapse."

There.

Different job.

Good.

East Hook lower service quay had lost twelve feet of retaining face overnight.

Not whole quay.

Section.

Old timber crib behind stone had rotted, one tide seam opened, then yesterday's rain and overnight wash took enough fill that front edge slumped.

No one injured.

Two handcarts lost.

One storage cage tilted into water.

And three businesses immediately disagreed over what counted as emergency recovery versus private property preservation.

Excellent morning.

Tavren pointed at map.

"We stabilize retrieval lane only. Harbor Works owns quay. We recover objects if authorized. We do not repair wall."

Nali added, "No one steps beyond red chalk. Ground under intact stone may not be intact."

Jerr had riggers there already.

Pella still absent.

Different diver today, **Oss Renn**, no relation to Dask unless universe hated me.

I did not ask.

Growth.

My assignment:

shore tally.

condition intake.

load sequence board.

Not crane command.

Not structural decision.

Tavren said, "If Works changes boundary, you rewrite board before line moves."

"Yes."

"If owner screams, you still rewrite board."

"Likely yes."

"Good."

We went.

Collapse looked worse up close.

Stone face had folded inward like broken teeth.

Water sucked through gaps.

Mud under surface moved brown with each surge.

A green-painted storage cage leaned half-submerged against remaining wall.

One handcart wheel stuck above water.

Second cart gone.

Three owners stood behind rope arguing before crew arrived.

**Lena Vos**, rope chandlery.

**Perrin Holt**, lamp-oil warehouse.

**Serr Arlo**, courier storage.

Lena wanted cage first because it held imported dry rope.

Perrin wanted submerged oil lockbox before water compromised seals.

Serr wanted courier dispatch chest because it contained route documents and customer deposits.

Harbor Works inspector **Toma Kess** wanted none moved until void edge was sounded.

Everybody had reason.

No obvious villain.

Again.

Toma put iron sounding bar against stone three feet behind red chalk.

Hollow.

Moved back another foot.

Solid.

Red line shifted.

I erased board.

Rewrote staging.

Lena said, "Every minute rope sits wet costs me."

Toma said, "Every minute worker stands on hollow quay costs leg."

That shut conversation for almost three seconds.

Then Perrin said, "My oil box is already underwater."

Serr said, "My chest has names and deposits."

Tavren looked at water.

"Recovery order follows access and hazard, not who shouts loudest."

Lena opened mouth.

"Shout if you want. Doesn't change line."

She closed it.

I liked him.

First problem was green cage.

Visible.

Accessible from water.

Heavy enough that crane needed clean angle.

Rigging team set sling from stable side.

Nali had me prepare condition lane because cage might split under lift.

I set tarps.

Tags.

Two empty baskets.

Crutches annoyed me immediately.

One hand for slate.

One hand unavailable because crutch.

Then switch.

Then brace slate against chest.

Then move.

Slow.

Nali walked past carrying pry bar and tags in both hands.

Wet-deck foot today again.

She noticed eyes.

"Work."

"Working."

"Stare after."

Fair.

Lift began.

Green cage came up crooked.

One lower corner caught broken stone.

Jerr stopped.

No drama.

Line held.

Oss reached from skiff, shifted sling angle.

Second lift.

Cage cleared.

Then bottom seam opened.

Rope coils started dropping.

Not expensive magic.

Just thirty years of gravity waiting.

Jerr yelled, "Catch basket!"

This was not my lane.

But catch basket was beside me.

I could move it.

I hooked one crutch over shoulder, grabbed basket with free hand and dragged, ugly and fast, into tarp lane while Nali caught second side.

Two coils landed in.

Third hit mud.

Fourth stayed cage.

Good enough.

No hero.

Just hands shortage.

Again.

With peg I could have carried basket instead of dragging.

Noted.

Later.

Cage owner Lena crossed arms.

"How much ruined?"

Nali said, "Not my decision. Condition first."

I recorded:

four rope coils visible.

Two basket-caught, wet.

One mud-contact.

One cage-retained.

No assumption about sale loss.

Lena hated that.

"They're wet."

"Yes."

"Write ruined."

"I can't establish ruined."

"You can see them."

"I can see wet."

She looked ready to murder epistemology.

Nali said, "He writes wet. You argue value with insurer."

Lena swore.

Fair.

Then oil lockbox.

Perrin's.

Smaller.

Submerged under collapsed cart frame.

Oss found it.

But before lift, charge screen from skiff gave faint amber on latch.

Perrin said, "It's lamp oil. No charge."

Nali said, "Box disagrees."

"It has anti-spark seal."

There.

Useful.

Not dangerous magic necessarily.

Anti-spark seal could retain tiny charge.

Nali changed handling class to low residual known-use if mark matched.

Mark did.

Lift approved with no opening.

I learned local hazard vocabulary without pretending surprise.

Then Serr's courier chest.

Divers couldn't find it.

That became problem.

Serr had seen it at midnight before collapse.

Said chained to inner post.

Oss found post.

Chain cut.

Chest absent.

Current could have moved it.

Could be under debris.

Could have been removed before collapse.

Could have drifted into basin.

Serr's face changed.

"It was there."

Toma said, "I believe you. Doesn't make it here now."

"There are deposits in it."

"How much?" Sori asked.

She had come after noon with Maro, mostly to see if I still had head.

Serr looked at her.

"Eleven customers. Fourteen copper total. Documents more important."

Not huge by Duskport market.

Huge if customers thought courier stole money.

He wanted full search immediately.

Tavren had contracted stabilization recovery until third bell.

Full basin search would mean extra diver time, likely push Merry Wake turn window, cost crew, maybe no result.

Again.

Human wants.

Correct procedure had no clean answer.

Serr said, "I'll pay."

Tavren said, "Not about only pay."

"Then what?"

"Diver limit. Current. Other booked work."

"So my customers lose deposits because you're busy?"

Tavren did not flinch.

"Maybe."

Serr laughed bitter.

"You all love maybe."

That hit.

Tessa.

Same line shape.

Different person.

I hated it.

Sori saw me notice.

I looked at collapse map.

Not for clever answer.

For actual options.

"Can Harbor Works sweep downstream grates?" I asked Toma.

"Already scheduled after wall secure."

"Today?"

"Likely before dusk."

"Can recovery mark chest description to them?"

"Yes."

"Can East Basin watch post?"

Tavren said, "Harbor watch can circulate missing property notice."

Serr said, "That's not search."

"No," I said.

I did not pretend.

"It's not."

He looked at me.

"Then don't sell it like one."

"I'm not."

Silence.

Better.

Tavren chose:

No extended diver search.

Current too poor near collapsed face.

One additional ten-minute sweep within safe lane only.

Then stop.

Harbor Works grate sweep + watch notice + recovery description.

Serr hated it.

Accepted because what else.

Ten minutes found nothing.

That stayed unresolved.

Good.

Around second bell, wind shifted.

Crane barge outside breakwater signaled Merry Wake window opening early.

Tavren had choice.

Keep all crew on quay collapse through third bell.

Or split and send recovery barge team to wreck now.

Short crew because Pella out.

Jerr said he could take three riggers plus Oss.

Nali said condition intake at yard could handle delayed returns.

Tavren looked at me.

"You can hold quay board with Toma?"

There.

More responsibility.

Not structural authority.

Not crane.

Board.

Records.

Owner sequence.

"Yes."

He looked at Nali.

She nodded.

"He can."

That meant something.

Tavren split crew.

He went Merry Wake with Jerr.

Nali stayed half bell, then returned yard for incoming.

I stayed quay with Toma and two recovery hands.

First time Tavren was not physically there.

No Vessa.

No Tavren.

Toma owned safety boundary.

I owned recovery board/tally.

Easy.

Until wall moved.

Not collapse.

Sound.

Deep wooden crack under stone.

Toma's head snapped.

"Back."

Everybody moved.

One owner didn't.

Perrin stepped toward oil box staging because he thought box was slipping.

I said, "Back."

He said, "It's moving."

"Back."

He took another step.

I did not lock in fully.

Didn't need retirement fund.

Just louder.

"Perrin. Back now."

Something in voice worked.

He stopped.

Toma grabbed his coat and pulled him behind second line.

Three seconds later one intact-looking paving slab dropped six inches into void.

Not dramatic explosion.

Worse.

Proof.

His oil box had not moved.

Shadow had.

Toma re-marked boundary another six feet.

Recovery halted.

That killed last cart attempt.

Perrin said nothing.

Then, quietly:

"Thank you."

I said, "Toma heard it."

"You yelled."

"Also true."

No sermon.

Work resumed only after Toma approved alternate lane.

We finished what could finish.

At third bell, Tavren returned wet and tired.

Merry Wake had produced second safe and one steering linkage.

No injuries.

Good.

He checked quay board.

Read every correction.

Serr missing chest notice.

Boundary shifts.

Canceled cart lift.

Perrin incident.

Green cage partial loss.

Then looked at me.

"You change safety line yourself?"

"No. Toma did. I rewrote board after."

"Tell owner ruined rope?"

"No. Wet/mud contact only."

"Tell courier chest stolen?"

"No. Missing after collapse."

"Direct Perrin?"

"Told him back after Toma called back."

Toma said, "He listened second time."

"Eventually," I said.

Tavren nodded.

That was review.

Then pay.

No custody inventory tonight.

Four copper.

Thirty-two to thirty-six.

There.

Trial total had become:

Two half-day.

Four first full.

Five second.

Four third.

Fifteen copper earned at Venn Marine Recovery.

Not fortune.

Real.

Tavren put coin pouch away.

"Trial done."

There.

I waited.

Didn't sell myself.

He hated that probably less.

"You staying Duskport?"

"For now."

"How long?"

"At least long enough to make bad financial decisions about leg."

Nali, beside him, snorted.

Tavren looked at left knee.

"Masta?"

"Yes."

"Travel?"

"Probably."

"Expensive."

"Yes."

"Good."

I blinked.

"Good?"

"Cheap limb that fails under load costs more."

Fair.

Then offer.

Not permanent.

Not guild.

Not charity.

**Open temporary recovery hand, condition/tally class.**

Five-day block.

Minimum three full assigned days if weather/work supports.

Base 3c useful records day.

4c when load tally assigned.

5c with signed evening custody inventory.

Same restrictions.

No diving.

No rigging authority.

No salvage claim rights.

If yard has no work, no pay.

If Greg leaves for fitting appointment, tell them before morning board if possible.

Tavren said, "You're useful."

Vessa phrase.

Different person.

Same high praise.

"I'll take it."

"Starts tomorrow second bell. Merry Wake if sea holds, East Hook inventory if not."

"Second bell?"

"You worked three early days. Sleep."

Beautiful employer.

Nali said, "Also Masta wants you tomorrow before first bell."

"Why?"

Not deposit.

Not fitting start.

Measurements.

"Cost?"

"Assessment included if you eventually buy. One bit if you waste her morning."

"That's fair."

Sori appeared from behind stacked cage.

"You're going."

"Apparently."

"Good."

I counted current money mentally.

Thirty-six copper.

Vale twenty-three.

Travel leg one silver plus eighteen.

Still far.

But now there was open work block.

And Masta wanted real measurements.

That changed target from fantasy shopping to project.

Dangerous.

Good.

We walked back toward Anchor's End.

Duskport smelled like salt, tar, and brewery smoke.

Somewhere Black Keel existed.

I did not go.

Growth.

Maro asked, "Beer?"

"No."

Dask said, "Could compare another label."

"No."

Sori said, "Miracle."

Then at hands.

Both occupied.

Tomorrow morning Masta would measure what could replace some of that occupation.

Not leg.

Tool.

Option.

Then second bell, back to work.

I liked shape of it.

Earn.

Measure.

Work.

Save.

Maybe fit.

Not dramatic.

Serious.

# CHAPTER 415

## THE CANDIDATE

Masta Venn measured everything.

That included things I had not known could be measured.

"Stand straight."

"I am."

"No. You're standing crutch-straight."

"Different?"

"Very."

She tapped left hip.

"You load away from this side before you think about it."

"Reasonable."

"Useful. Also problem."

There.

Morning.

Before first bell.

Hark & Venn smelled like leather and hot glue and whatever oil Masta used on brass fittings.

I had eaten.

She asked.

Apparently that mattered.

I had also not had beer.

She did not ask.

Probably because Duskport could smell its own crimes.

Masta had cleared long bench and brought out strips of cloth, wax pencil, calipers, leather tape, a wooden measuring fork, two temporary support blocks, and one expression that suggested I was furniture with opinions.

"Pants up."

I rolled left leg cloth above knee.

She looked at stump.

"Any soreness from yard?"

"No skin breakdown. Mild pressure after long crutch day."

"Where?"

I pointed.

Lateral upper edge.

She marked it.

"Scar sensitivity?"

"Low."

"End pressure?"

"Depends."

"Good answer."

She pressed gently.

Different places.

Asked each time.

No ceremony.

No sympathy face.

Good.

Circumference at several heights.

Length from knee line.

Knee flexion.

Extension.

Hip line.

Pelvis level.

Right leg length.

Crutch height.

Even shoe sole thickness.

"Why shoe?"

"Because if I build left side to imaginary floor and right boot adds half inch, you walk like roof."

"Fair."

She had me stand between rails.

Right foot centered.

Hands lightly on rails.

Then she placed padded block under left stump and raised it by thin wooden plates.

One.

Two.

Three.

"Tell me when pelvis feels level."

"That's not reliable."

"Exactly. Tell me anyway."

I hated craft people.

"There."

She looked.

"You're wrong."

"Excellent test."

"You think level is low left because that's your normal."

There.

That landed.

She raised one more plate.

"Now?"

"Too high."

"Good."

Dropped half.

"Now?"

I waited.

Body argued.

Then settled.

"Strange."

"That means close."

She checked hips with measuring bar.

"Close."

Interesting.

Current body had spent years building a map around absence.

A fitted leg would not simply add support.

It would force map to change.

Masta wrote numbers.

"You overprotect left side."

"I have no foot there."

"Yes. That's why."

"Insightful."

"Pay me silver and I have more."

I liked her less.

She moved on.

Temporary socket shell next.

Not finished socket.

Open leather-and-canvas cup with straps.

"This is not fitting."

"You keep saying that."

"Because people hear 'measurement' and think they're walking by lunch."

"I'm not people."

"Worse."

She wrapped stump in thin sock, seated temporary cup, tightened straps one at time.

Pressure.

Odd.

Not pain.

Contained.

That was best word.

I had spent years with air below knee.

Now something held shape around it.

Body disliked novelty.

Not exactly fear.

Attention.

Every nerve suddenly had meeting.

"Pain?"

"No."

"Numbness?"

"No."

"Burning?"

"No."

"Pressure?"

"Yes."

"Where?"

I pointed.

She marked shell.

Loosened.

Shifted pad.

Retightened.

"Better?"

"Different."

"Useful word."

Then support post.

Just plain adjustable wooden shaft under socket.

No foot.

No finished hardware.

She locked it to rail fixture so it could not slide.

"Load ten percent."

"How do I know ten?"

"You don't. That's why I watch."

Great.

I shifted.

Right leg immediately tried to keep almost everything.

"More left."

I shifted.

"Too much shoulder."

"Shoulders aren't on leg."

"Your whole body is on leg."

There.

Again.

I relaxed arms.

Shifted pelvis.

Pressure moved down temporary socket.

Not bad.

Not comfortable.

Real.

"Hold."

I held.

Five breaths.

Ten.

Fifteen.

Muscles I used constantly still found new complaint.

Left hip working differently.

Lower back adjusting.

Right calf relaxing slightly.

Hands doing almost nothing.

That was the thing.

Hands.

Both free on rails rather than bearing body.

I lifted right hand completely.

Then left.

Masta immediately said, "Don't perform."

"I wasn't."

"You were about to."

Probably.

I put hands back.

She had seen enough.

"Travel leg, yes."

There.

Simple.

"Not basic peg?"

"You could use one. Wrong tool if you plan roads, wet yards, ships, stairs, carrying, fighting, whatever nonsense face says."

"Face says nothing."

"Face says expensive mistakes."

Rude city.

She pulled stool.

"Your main problems aren't stump length or knee. Those are good. Your problem is habit. You unload left side before danger exists. Pelvis sits a little low left when tired. Right side overworks. Crutches reinforce some of that because they make it functional."

"So leg fixes it."

"No."

Of course.

"Leg gives you chance to train different pattern. If you wear badly, you can build worse pattern faster."

"Good."

"Also socket volume will change during day. Yard swelling. Heat. Salt. Long standing. First month means adjustments."

"How many?"

"Enough."

"Helpful."

"Could be three. Could be nine."

There.

Not product.

Process.

I asked, "Would you still quote one silver eighteen?"

She looked at measurements.

"Yes for travel work build as described. Maybe plus small material difference if you choose reinforced side stay after trial shell. I don't know yet."

"Deposit still twenty?"

"Yes."

Thirty-six copper in purse.

Could do it.

Still no.

Not yet.

"How much do I need liquid before you think I'm not being stupid?"

She smiled slightly.

First time.

"That's not my job."

"You had opinion last time."

"Last time you'd have one copper. Easy opinion."

Fair.

I thought.

Lodging.

Food.

Return route.

Vale.

Uncertain workdays.

Silver balance unknown in copper terms because denomination structure here still not mine to invent.

Twenty-copper deposit would leave sixteen.

Better than one.

Still maybe thin if work stopped.

"Not today," I said.

Masta nodded.

No disappointment.

"Good. Measurements stay six weeks before I remeasure everything. Major body change, injury, skin problem, come sooner."

"No charge?"

"Not if you eventually buy. One bit if you disappear forever and wasted morning."

"Threatening."

"Business."

She handed me small card.

**GREG / LEFT BKA / TRAVEL-WORK CANDIDATE / BASELINE TAKEN**

Below that numbers I did not understand yet.

Real.

Not mine.

Not leg.

Still real.

I put it in shoulder bag.

"Second bell," she said.

"Work."

"Then stop standing here."

Good morning.

East Hook at second bell had no wreck lift.

Wind still wrong outside breakwater.

Instead Tavren pointed inland.

"North Pier warehouse strike."

I looked at him.

"Strike?"

"Not labor strike. Crane strike."

"Ah."

"Hook hit upper beam. Part of loading gallery collapsed. No injuries. Cargo trapped. Harbor inspector cleared one lane."

Different again.

Good.

North Pier warehouse belonged to **Kerrin & Sons Provisioning**.

Three floors.

Stone lower.

Timber upper loading gallery over quay.

One crane boom had swung in gust during morning transfer and smashed through gallery corner.

No one hurt because warning bell sounded before secondary collapse.

Now half upper platform hung at angle.

Sacks, crates, two copper-bound ice cabinets, and one long white case remained inside cleared zone.

Harbor inspector owned structure.

Kerrin owner wanted perishables first.

Insurance assessor wanted nothing moved until damage plates finished.

Dock master wanted quay lane reopened before evening tide because two provisioning ships were due.

Of course.

People.

Tavren said, "We remove what inspector authorizes. Greg, board and tally. Nali condition. Sesh rigging."

New rigger **Sesh Om**.

Short woman, enormous forearms, braided beard ornaments despite having no beard.

Actually hair braids tied under chin because wind.

Looked beard-like.

I did not comment.

Growth.

Inspector **Meren Cole** had chalked green retrieval corridor across lower floor.

Anything outside green stayed.

Owner **Jase Kerrin** hated green.

"Ice cabinets first."

Meren said, "One is outside corridor."

"Contents are worth thirty copper by tonight."

"Floor under it is cracked."

"Can rig from above."

Sesh said, "No."

Jase looked at her.

"You haven't looked."

"Looked. Still no."

Efficient.

Second cabinet was inside green.

We took that first.

Then food crates.

Then long white case.

White case had no obvious ownership mark.

Just three blue dots and brass end caps.

Nali stopped intake.

"Cold?"

I held hand near without touching.

"Slightly."

She screened.

Green.

Then amber at center.

"Not open here."

Jase said, "That's mine."

Nali said, "Mark?"

"Provisioning inventory."

"Paper?"

He called clerk.

Clerk brought manifest.

Long white case listed as **LEASED PRESERVATION ROD / NORTH COAST COLDWORKS / RETURN DUE 17TH**.

Not Jase's property.

Lease equipment.

Interesting.

"Need Coldworks custody notice," I said.

Sori would be proud.

Nali nodded.

Jase did not.

"I need it working."

"Maybe," I said.

He glared.

"You people love maybe?"

Tessa line hit memory.

There.

Different person.

Same frustration.

I did not get defensive.

"Yes," I said. "Because I don't know if it works."

He stared.

Then looked away.

No clever fix.

We tagged leased equipment and sent runner.

Meanwhile second ice cabinet remained outside green.

Jase kept watching it.

Thirty copper by tonight.

Real loss.

Meren kept line.

Real collapse risk.

No one became wrong.

At third bell, upper platform creaked.

Not loud.

Enough.

Meren raised fist.

Everyone stopped.

Then another crack.

Sesh said, "Out."

We moved.

I backed on crutches.

Bad direction for speed.

Current body knew.

Turn.

Right foot.

Crutches.

Move.

Nali was ahead carrying board and pry bar.

Both hands occupied.

Her left work leg planted and pushed clean.

Mine did not exist.

I moved anyway.

Fast enough.

Gallery corner dropped another foot after we cleared.

Dust.

Boards.

One sack burst.

No injury.

Meren closed green corridor entirely.

Jase swore.

Then stood very still.

His second ice cabinet was still inside.

Thirty copper maybe dying behind unsafe floor.

Nobody told him procedure was good news.

Tavren said, "We stop."

Jase said, "Can you recover from quay side?"

Sesh looked.

"Maybe after brace crew. Not now."

There it was again.

Maybe.

Human word.

Not cowardice.

Not answer.

Sometimes only honest bridge between no and yes.

Jase rubbed face.

"Fine."

He did not mean fine.

We packed.

Short day because structure closed.

Tavren still had another yard job after fourth bell, but only two hands needed.

He picked Nali and Sesh.

I expected no pay or maybe partial.

Temporary block said assigned days, not guaranteed full.

Tavren looked at board.

"Records useful. Half day plus stop not your fault. Three copper."

I blinked.

"Full base?"

"You were assigned full day. Harbor closure ended it. Yard absorbs closure."

Good employer again.

"Thanks."

"Don't thank payroll."

Thirty-six to thirty-nine.

There.

Thirty-nine copper.

Still no deposit.

Still target.

But card in bag now.

Baseline.

Candidate.

That word did something.

Not ownership.

Not promise.

Direction.

At Anchor's End, Dask was drawing three mirror diagrams on napkin.

Sori had letter.

Not home.

Harbor court runner.

She looked up when I entered.

"Harven made hearing."

There.

One thread.

"Outcome?"

"Appeal partially granted. Labor levy reduced from six months to two. Work ban stayed, review in ninety days."

Not clean.

Of course.

"He saw her?"

Sori nodded.

"Yes."

That mattered more than ruling for him maybe.

"Mira?"

"Runner note says quarantine accepted before third bell. Birds held observation overnight, contract not automatically void."

Two threads.

Not miracles.

Consequences moved.

"Tessa?"

Sori shook head.

No.

Still nothing.

Good.

Not good.

Honest.

Maro came in behind me with food.

"Work?"

"Three copper. Half day. Warehouse tried to become floor."

"Successful?"

"Partly."

He nodded like that was normal answer now.

I pulled Masta card from bag.

Set it on table.

Sori read.

**TRAVEL-WORK CANDIDATE / BASELINE TAKEN**

Her face changed.

"Oh."

"Yeah."

Dask immediately leaned.

"What are measurements?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Because you'll graph me."

"I wasn't going to."

"You absolutely were."

Maro looked at card.

"Deposit?"

"No."

Sori nodded.

"Good."

"Still good?"

"Comforting."

"I know."

"Good."

There.

Yes.

Real enough to measure.

Not real enough to own.

That was fine.

Probably.

Tomorrow board might have work.

Might not.

Five-day block had four more days.

Thirty-nine copper.

One silver plus eighteen.

Badly.

Earn.

Save.

Listen.
